opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important generalization problem is generalizing across the physical world itself: new environments, new objects, new tasks, and eventually new embodiments.

In language models, generalization came almost for free once we had enough data, because the internet already contains a huge, diverse record of human text. Physical AI doesn't have that. A robot trained in one kitchen, with one lighting setup, one set of cups and one arm, often fails when you move it to another kitchen. The space of physical situations is enormous, the long tail is very long, and collecting real interaction data is slow, expensive and sometimes unsafe.

So the core question is how to get a model that understands physics and cause and effect well enough to handle situations it has never seen. That means knowing that an object falls when you let go, that liquid spills when a cup tips, and that a soft object deforms differently from a rigid one. Memorizing trajectories isn't enough.

That's a big part of why I'm excited about world models. If you can build a model that has learned, from large amounts of video and sensor data, how the world evolves in response to actions, you can use it as a kind of simulator of reality. You can generate the rare and dangerous cases, vary the environments and the objects, and train and evaluate policies at a scale you could never reach with physical robots alone.

Then there's a second layer, which is generalization across embodiments. Today, every new robot body almost means starting over. Ideally, the knowledge of how the world works should be shared, and only a thinner layer should adapt to the specific body: a humanoid, a robot arm, or a car.

To sum up: generalize over environments, over the long tail of situations, and over embodiments. Underneath all of that is the data problem. We need a scalable way to get physically grounded experience, and I think world models plus simulation, combined with real data, is the most promising path.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots trained in limited settings failing in new ones, and identifies handling never-seen situations as the core problem. Its references to training and adapting policies convey transfer of learned behavior to new situations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. If I had to pick one, I'd say the hardest and most important generalization problem for Physical AI is generalizing across the physical world itself, across the long tail of situations a robot or an autonomous vehicle will encounter that were never in its training data.

Let me explain why this is different from what we solved in language. In language, we had the internet. Trillions of tokens of human text were already sitting there, and they cover an enormous slice of human experience. So when you train a large language model, you get this remarkable generalization almost for free, because the data distribution is so broad.

Physical AI does not have that. There is no internet of robot experience. Every robot that exists today has collected a tiny amount of data, in a few labs, in a few kitchens, in a few warehouses. And the physical world is far more diverse than text. Lighting changes, objects deform, friction varies, a cable gets tangled in a way nobody anticipated. The space of states is essentially infinite, and the cost of getting it wrong is physical. You cannot just regenerate the answer.

So the generalization problem I care most about has a few layers. The first is embodiment. Can a model trained mostly on one robot body transfer to a different arm, a different gripper, a humanoid with different kinematics? Right now that transfer is weak. The second is environment. Can a policy that works in one warehouse work in a hospital it has never seen? And the third, which I think is the deepest, is physics itself. Does the model actually understand that if I push a cup off the table it falls, that liquids pour, that a stack of boxes can topple? Or has it just memorized visual patterns?

That is why I have spent so much energy on world foundation models. The idea is to give Physical AI something analogous to what the internet gave language models: a general-purpose understanding of how the physical world evolves. If a model can predict what happens next in video, under different actions, in millions of diverse scenarios, then it has a prior about physics and causality. You can use that model to generate synthetic experience, to evaluate policies safely, and to let a robot imagine the consequences of an action before it takes it.

I will also say that simulation and real data are not competitors here. The path forward is a flywheel. You use world models and simulation to cover the long tail you cannot collect in reality, you deploy in the real world, you collect the failures, and you feed those back in. Generalization comes from that loop, not from any single dataset.

So if you ask me what success looks like, it is a robot that walks into a space it has never seen, with objects it has never handled, and behaves sensibly on the first try. We are not there. But I believe the recipe is now visible, and that is what makes this moment so exciting.

r001.rationale: The response identifies generalizing to situations absent from training data as the central problem, and describes whether a learned policy can act in unseen environments and with unfamiliar objects. It also emphasizes that robots have only collected tiny amounts of data.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important problem is generalizing to situations the system has never encountered before. In the physical world, even a simple task can look very different from one environment to another. The objects change, the lighting changes, and the same object can behave differently depending on its weight or friction.

Imagine asking a robot to pick up a cup. We don’t want it to succeed only with the cups and positions it saw during training. We want it to understand enough about grasping and physical interaction to handle a new cup, recognize when its grip is slipping, and adjust.

So the challenge goes beyond visual recognition. It’s connecting perception to action and predicting what happens when you act. And when that prediction is wrong, can you use the feedback to recover? To me, that ability to transfer what you’ve learned and adapt in an unfamiliar situation is central to Physical AI.

r001.rationale: The response says the system should transfer learned grasping and physical interaction to new cups and unfamiliar situations, linking perception to action and adapting through feedback. This clearly conveys generalizing a learned observation-to-action mapping to unseen situations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important problem is generalizing from the environments where we collect training data to the environments where we actually want a robot to operate. If you train a robot to perform a task in one kitchen, can it perform that task in a different kitchen, with different objects, lighting, and layouts?

That requires more than recognizing what things look like. The robot needs to understand how its actions change the world. An object might look familiar but have a different weight or friction, so the robot has to adapt through interaction.

The key question is whether we can learn representations of the physical world that transfer across those variations, so that every new environment doesn’t become a new data-collection project. Simulation and world models could help, but ultimately the test is whether that knowledge leads to reliable behavior in unfamiliar real-world situations.

r001.rationale: It describes generalizing from training environments to unfamiliar operating environments, illustrated by transferring a task learned in one kitchen to a different kitchen. Its discussion of adapting actions through interaction supports the observation-to-action transfer target.
